newsitem.title: BOTSWANA: Air Botswana turns in profit, mulls privatisation.
newsitem.headline: Air Botswana turns in profit, mulls privatisation.

text.p: Air Botswana on Friday reported its first ever profit and indicated it would soon start looking for privatisation partners.
"Its time to start acting like a private airline," general manager Joshua Galeforolwe told journalists at a news conference.
For the year ended March 31, operating revenue increased by 22 percent to 51.03 million pula ($195.5 million) while operating costs rose by 10 percent to 47.36 million.

"I am pleased to report a net profit of 3.02 million pula. Air Botswana is now one of the four profitable airlines in Africa, joining Kenya and Ethiopian Airways and South Africa's Comair," Galeforolwe said.

At the end of 1993, the government re-capitalised the then loss-making Air Botswana on the understanding there would be no more loans or capital injections. Privatisation would come once the airline became profitable.
"The Minister of Finance told us we would have to sink or swim and if we stayed afloat we would be privatised," Galeforolwe said.
Management took up the challenge and managed to cut losses from 18.7 million pula to 2.1 million during 1994 and 1995.
The airline was completely restructured with the focus on the development of the Botswana domestic market and flights to neighbouring countries.
"We shifted focus to concentrate on the local market and the closer regional market. We are developing a niche market as a feeder operator (to international flights)."
Management also focused on diversifying revenue sources.
"We identified a need for aircraft maintenance in the region and now have contracts with the Ministry of Agriculture to manage its fleet and with Zambia Airways to service its ATRs," Galeforole said.
Continued cost control, the re-negotiation of contracts and route rationalisation saw losses trimmed back to 1.8 million pula in 1996 and now a first ever profit in 1997.

Galeforolwe said the government was currently looking at partial-privatisation but at present, bilateral air services agreements between Botswana and the countries Air Botswana flies to, specify that the designated carrier must be majority-owned and controlled by nationals of Botswana.
"Whatever proportion is hived-off, the government plus nationals must continue to own a majority.
"Our view is that we need a strong partner who flies from the regional hub (Johannesburg) and to whom we can feed traffic," he said.
